title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Agent Economics** (Vol III). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

A model whose tokens cost a tenth as much looks like a large saving on the provider's invoice and can still raise the price of every task the agent finishes. Token charges are only part of the account. An attempt also holds a sandbox open while its tools run, invokes tests and external services, waits for shared capacity, and may end in human review, and an attempt that fails pays for all of it without producing anything that ships.

nodes.label: The Bill Behind an Accepted Repair

rows: **Cohort cost per accepted task**
Measured cost per accepted task is the sum of every initiated task's account, each charge in exactly one category, divided by the distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.
**Prefix-cache pricing and compaction payback**

Ideal prefix reuse bills the quadratic re-send at the cached rate, which lowers its coefficient without removing it, so a compaction pays back only after enough turns to recover its rewrite and lost cache.
**Critical-path acceleration ceiling**
A speedup g applied to a fraction f of the measured critical path gives T' = T[(1-f) + f/g] and a ceiling of 1/(1-f), which a baseline profile reveals before anything is bought.
**Cascade and routing pricing**
A cascade's cost and acceptance are reach-weighted sums, so savings come from the early-exit rate, every reached gate charges whether or not its candidate passes, and fail-through harm is priced in.
**Trajectory goodput**

Accepted tasks per unit time is the platform's deliverable, so sustaining goodput G at acceptance alpha requires admitting G/alpha trajectories and any change that lowers acceptance raises offered load.
**Queueing cost of utilization**
Near saturation queueing wait grows like rho/(1-rho), so a modest throughput gain from higher utilization costs a multiple in wait that compounds across every serial step of a trajectory.
**Budget conservation**

Every budget account in the tree keeps budget = settled + reserved + free under atomic, logged transitions, so a delegation tree conserves spending and a stopped child keeps its reservation until its late bills settle.
**Architecture pricing with human fallback**

Deterministic code, a fixed workflow, a bounded loop, and delegation are compared under one acceptance contract by cost per resolved task including human fallback, not by automated cost per automated acceptance.
**Dedicated capacity break-even**
Owning capacity beats an API at a delivered utilization u* = F / (3600 R (P_eff - v)), not at a token price.
**Speculative decoding profitability**
Speculative decoding pays only when the accepted-draft rate shortens the output-bound critical path by more than draft and verification work add to the bill.
**Adaptation payback**
A one-time adaptation investment recovers its cost after N* = C_adapt / (C_base - C_adapted) tasks, never if the per-task saving is nonpositive, and only while acceptance stays equal.
